keyTakeaways: Accessibility captions make important non-speech sound information readable for the audience.
Stage directions guide the production; audience captions may need wording that describes the sound in the actual staging.
In normal Next/Previous navigation, the operator console skips stage-direction cues while Accessibility Captions remain in the cue sequence.
SurtitleLive adds one pair of brackets for display; the production team decides which sounds matter to the audience.

faq.question: What are accessibility captions in theatre?
faq.answer: Accessibility captions turn important auditory information into readable text for the audience. They can describe significant sound effects, music changes, alarms, offstage activity and other audio events that help people understand the performance.

faq.question: How are accessibility captions different from dialogue subtitles?
faq.answer: Dialogue subtitles primarily represent what characters say. Accessibility captions can represent meaningful audio that nobody speaks, such as knocking, breaking glass, a warning siren, a crowd approaching or music stopping.

faq.question: Why not use stage directions directly?
faq.answer: Stage directions are written primarily for making the performance. Accessibility captions are written for the audience. A stage direction may need to be rewritten to describe the sound as it is actually heard, and many stage directions should not be shown to the audience at all.

faq.question: Are Accessibility Captions skipped when Skip Stage Directions is on?
faq.answer: No. During normal Next/Previous navigation, stage-direction cues are skipped while Accessibility Captions remain in sequence and can be sent to the audience. Directly jumping to a cue is a separate action.

glossary.definition: Audience text that communicates meaningful sound information, including sounds nobody speaks.
A script instruction written primarily to guide the making of a performance.
Text prepared to give spectators information they may not receive through sound.
Audible information such as a knock, alarm, music change or offstage activity.
A category the production team selects for a line instead of having the software infer it.
